INTRODUCTION

1
Nettie Richardson, formerly Romaniuk,
died December 8, 1991 at the age of 80 years.  She was survived by her second
husband of approximately eight years, Arthur George Richardson, and her only
child, the child of her first marriage, the 64 year old plaintiff.  At the
trial the deceased was referred to as Mrs. Romaniuk, Mrs. Richardson, the
deceased, the mother, and so on.  I will refer to her as Nettie.

2
By her last will dated November 1, 1991,
made five weeks before her death, Nettie left a life estate to her second
husband in her home at 5018 Montrose Street, in Port Alberni, which residence
she and her first husband, Peter Romaniuk, had constructed and occupied since
the mid 1960s until Mr. Romaniuk's death.  Her second husband died April 3,
1993.  She left 10% of her estate to Canadian Guide Dogs for the Blind, and 10%
to Shriners Hospital for Crippled Children.  She left $5,000.00 to her
neighbours, Joseph and Toots Schultz, and the balance of her estate equally to
her 78 year old sister, Virginia Ekdahl, and her nephew, Stefan Vatamaniuck.
Ekdahl and Vatamaniuck are also Nettie's executors and trustees.

3
Nettie expressly disinherited her only
child, the plaintiff, stating in her will:

5.I
make no gift to my daughter Katherine Gieni because she attempted to deny my
inheritance following the death of my first husband.

Hence, the plaintiff brings this
action under the
Wills Variation Act
, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 435.  At trial
she said that she wanted, or hoped to recover, Nettie's fancy cups or dishes,
one-half of her Royal Albert dish set, her father's tools and her
"father's home".  In his submissions her counsel said that the
plaintiff seeks two-thirds of Nettie's estate.

4
Nettie's small and hard earned estate
has a net value of approximately $167,000.00.  It includes savings of
$44,803.41, and $17,412.62, being made up of interest, rent, and other monies
received by the estate since Nettie's death.  The expenses paid out of those
monies total $10,104.56.  It also includes her Montrose Street home, which has
an appraised value of $114,500.00, and personal goods having a value of
$500.00.

5
In her earlier will dated February 8,
1983, Arthur George Richardson and Virginia Ekdahl were the executors and
trustees.  Her beneficiaries were her second husband, Arthur George Richardson,
her sister, Virginia Ekdahl, and her grandchildren, Cheryl Lynn Gieni, David Peter
Gieni, Gregory Kim Gieni, Kerry George Gieni, and Carol Corrine Gieni, all
children of the plaintiff.  The plaintiff was not named as a beneficiary in the
first will.  The grandchildren are not mentioned in the present will, with
which we are concerned.

6
The defendants Mr. and Mrs. Schultz for
obvious reasons were not represented at trial, although they filed a joint
statement of defence together with the defendants, Vatamaniuck and Ekdahl, who
are the primary defendants, and Mrs. Schultz gave evidence.  Similarly, the two
charities were not represented at trial, and simply took the usual passive
position.

7
The general issues, as stated by counsel
for the plaintiff, are:

(1)Did
Nettie have a moral duty toward the plaintiff to make some provision for her by
her will?  Was there an obligation to provide?

(2)Whether
Nettie's reasons for disinheriting the plaintiff were valid and rational.

8
The plaintiff pleads that Nettie did not
make adequate provision for her proper maintenance or support, in breach of her
moral duty to her; and that she is in need.  The primary defendants, who I will
call the defendants, deny the plaintiff's need or that the will did not make
adequate provision for the proper maintenance and support of the plaintiff.
Alternatively, the defendants say that if the will did not make adequate
provision, it is not just or equitable that any provision for the plaintiff
should be made out of Nettie's estate.  The main defence is contained in
paragraph 8 of the defence which is as follows:

8.In
further answer to the whole of the Plaintiff's claim the Defendants say that
the Plaintiff has disentitled herself from receiving maintenance or support
from the deceased estate by reason of her character or conduct towards the
deceased, particulars of which are:

(a)Attempting
to deprive, or in the alternative, depriving the deceased of property that in
justice, should have passed to the deceased either shortly before or following
the death of Peter Romaniuk, to whom the deceased was (since 1929) married at
the time of his death on the 22nd of November 1977; and

(b)Suing
the deceased in this Honourable Court by Writ issued in this Honourable Court
on the 24th of January, 1979, alleging wrongful appropriation of assets of
Peter Romaniuk that the Plaintiff alleged should have gone to her; and

(c)In
ignoring the deceased and refusing to be civil to her or to visit with her and
refusing the deceased access to the Plaintiff's children, following the death
of Peter Romaniuk through to the deceased's death.

THE EVIDENCE

9
Nettie and Peter Romaniuk met in
Saskatchewan in the late 1920s, and were married in 1929.  The plaintiff was
born on September 14, 1930.  The family spent the depression in Saskatchewan,
eking out a living as best they could.  Apparently Mr. Romaniuk was not able to
find work all the time.  He did find work at times, digging graves and working
for an oil company.  Nettie usually was able to find work as a house and school
cleaner, and later in a drycleaning business.

10
The family moved to Port Alberni in 1942,
where Mr. Romaniuk found work in a lumber mill.  Nettie found work in a plywood
mill for four years, and then worked in a hospital for 20 years.  Because her
parents worked shift work, the plaintiff was often home alone.  While she loved
her father and her mother, she favoured her father.

11
The plaintiff left school after grade 9.
She worked in a restaurant, then at Woodward's, and then a plywood plant.  She
married in May of 1951 and had five children "the grandchildren", all
of whom are adults.  Her husband was a heavy equipment operator until the late
1970s, when they bought a ranch or farm in the Fort St. John area.  They still
live on and work the farm.

12
The plaintiff said that at least
initially her mother got along with her husband quite well.  They used to go
fishing together, in a boat which they all purchased "in
partnership".  Her husband also got along with her father, who helped her
husband build their first home in Port Alberni.  Her husband also helped her
father build her parents' home in Port Alberni, the Montrose Street home.

13
Her father died in November of 1977.  She
had not noticed that he was ill, although Nettie had told her that he was
getting very forgetful.  She first saw her father's will at a solicitor's
office after her father had died.  She was the executrix and the residual
beneficiary.  She went to her father's bank to see what monies were in his account.
She was told that all of the monies had been withdrawn.  She, her husband and
her daughter-in-law, then went to see Nettie to find out what had happened to
the monies.  She says that Nettie became angry with her, and told her that it
was none of her business.  Nettie would never give her any explanation.

14
She eventually was shown her father's
cancelled cheques, by which the funds were withdrawn.  In her opinion the
signatures on the cheques were not her father's.  Again, Nettie told her that
it was none of her business.  So she went to a lawyer and eventually sued
Nettie.  This is when her relationship with Nettie began to deteriorate,
according to her.

15
Her father's estate was quite small.  Her
parents held the Montrose Street property in joint tenancy.  They also had a
joint bank account which contained approximately $23,000.00.  There had been
approximately $7,100.00 in her father's own bank account, and he had bonds
worth $3,000.00 or $4,000.00.

16
She was asked by her counsel why she let
the action against Nettie go to trial.  She said it was because her mother
called her father a "Jew", and she wanted to clear his name.  She
said that Nettie also told her that before his death he was throwing money
around like it was going out of style.  The witness said that she didn't think
that that was right, that "my father would not do that, regardless of how
rich he was."

17
It is common ground that her action
against Nettie proceeded to trial before Melvin, C.C.J., as he then was, on
April 8, 1980.  Her recollection is that Melvin, J. held that while her father
may have signed the cheques (with assistance) it was not his act, i.e. he was not
competent to do so.  The transactions were therefore set aside.  However,
Melvin, J. also held for Nettie on her counterclaim under the
Testator's
Family Maintenance Act
, and awarded the whole of her father's estate to
Nettie.

18
Counsel for the plaintiff asked her
again, why she would "go to all this trouble for $7,100.00?"  My
rough note of her answer is:

I didn't really want the
$7,100.00.  I wanted my dad's name cleared.  She was telling everyone,
including the grandchildren, what a mean, vindictive man he was, and he
wasn't.  I didn't want the money.

19
The plaintiff says that at the time she
was living part-time in Fort St. John, looking after a nearby ranch.  They had
loaned one Alvin Cantlon, the sum of $35,000.00 in order to assist him to buy
the ranch in 1977.  Mr. Cantlon did not repay them the $35,000.00, and
eventually they ended up buying the ranch from him.  They still work the ranch
today.

20
Counsel for the plaintiff then expressly
dealt with the further reasons why Nettie disinherited the plaintiff, according
to the evidence of the defendant Virginia Ekdahl given at discovery.  The first
is the assertion that the plaintiff influenced her father in the changing of
his will in her favour.  The second is that her relationship with Nettie soured
initially, when she and her husband tried unsuccessfully to persuade Nettie to
loan them $40,000.00.  The third reason given by Nettie to Ekdahl, was that the
plaintiff interfered with her relationship with her grandchildren, including
preventing her from going to at least two grandchildren's weddings.  The
plaintiff said that she never heard of any of these matters or reasons before.
Mrs. Ekdahl testified to them at discovery.  She acknowledged that Nettie did
not attend her daughter Carol's wedding on August 12, 1989.  When asked why the
witness said, referring to Nettie, "she said I would not allow her to come
and that I didn't send her an invitation.  Carol sent her the
invitation."  She expected her to come.  And she understood that she was
coming.

21
The plaintiff was asked about her
relationship with Nettie between 1977 and 1980.  She said that during that time
she and her husband lived on the farm.  They did not have a phone, and the farm
was some 80 miles from Fort St. John.  When asked whether she had any
communication with Nettie during that period of time she said that they had
written to each other "about three times each year."  She kept two of
Nettie's letters and they are in evidence.  She discarded her other letters,
when she answered them.

22
The first letter is dated July, and I am
satisfied that it was written in 1989, approximately one month before the
wedding of the grandchild, Carol, who then became Carol Bye.  Nettie commences
the letter with:

George and I hoped
our relations will have healed by now!

And after referring to one of the
grandchildren, Greg, she said:

I don't think the
children should of (sic) been mixed in the situation
.  It is (sic) been so long now.  I
don't see where the fault fell on me only.  Kaye I have never revealed to you
many many things your Dad and I went through.  I know he went to you, which I
didn't when things went wrong.  I was taught by Mother and Dad that children
shouldn't be mixed in their parents (sic) affairs which I believe in.  I want
to apologize to you George for saying the words I did say but I was also very
hurt about the whole thing.
I hope you can understand how many years of
hard labour I worked to make something
.

And:

This I want to tell you
that your Dad Kaye was ill and was halluzanating (sic) the last year of his
life you can ask his Drs. Kozheghi and Specialist from Nanaimo.  Your Dad told
them himself that he doesn't know whats (sic) wrong, he fears people braking (sic)
in through the windows.  I took him to Duncan to a Brain Specialist and he
examined him and told him to his face that a part of his brain at the back was
dying for not getting enough oxygen through his hardening of his arteries.

And with regard to her husband's
estate she said:

As for the estate he
wanted to leave everything to you.  How can a man do a thing like that when our
life was normal like any others with ups and downs.  He had said that no other
man should have pleasure of his labour.  I know how he felt as he worked very
hard, but, that's life you can't control after a death.

With regard to Carol's wedding she
said:

Carol and Michael are
nice kids.  We took them out to a dinner for their engagement and she has told
us
they would like us to attend their wedding
.

We would love to she
said to speak to you about it, My George would really like to meet you all.
He's a wonderfull (sic) man and he hopes we can all be a closer family
.

And she ended her letter with the
sentence:

Kaye if you want to
write us.  We'd love to attend Carol and Mikes (sic) wedding
.

(My emphasis)

And it is clear to me that by her
letter Nettie was again attempting to reconcile her relationship with the
plaintiff and her husband, and to obtain permission from the plaintiff to go to
Carol's wedding.  I also observe here that this letter does not suggest to me
that the plaintiff had written to Nettie, or had tried to reconcile with her,
prior to the letter being sent.

23
The second letter was found in an
envelope postmarked February 6, 1981.  She believes that it is the wrong
envelope for the letter.  She believes that the letter was written some time
after Christmas of 1987, because she and her husband were only in Port Alberni
at Christmas time on two occasions, after they went to the farm.

24
The letter is quite short, and is as
follows:

I am sorry I didnt (sic)
have time to talk to you at Xmas.  When you came over these people were invited
long ago to come and spend some time with us on Boxing day.  They had us at
their houses the previous years so it was our turn.  I wanted to give you your
Dads (sic) papers then and again when David went to visit you.  He had no other
papers.  You might need some of them in the future.  We are fine, but I had a
whole year as not too well!  Kaye let me know when you receive these papers.
Mom

P.S. Its (sic) time
we buried the hatchet!

(My emphasis)

25
The witness was referred to the statement
"it's time we buried the hatchet".  She said that Nettie always said
this in her letters to her; that they always responded that there was no
hatchet to bury.  She believes that her last letter to Nettie was in 1989, just
before Carol's wedding.  She also said that she responded to the first letter
referred to.  It will be seen that I have some difficulty with this evidence.

26
She referred to the first letter as
"an unusual letter", in which Nettie was trying to explain certain
things to her, i.e.:

It's been so long now.
I don't see where the fault fell on me only.  Kay I have never revealed to you
many things your Dad and I went through. ...

She says that she found the letter
kind of strange, that Nettie's other letters were not like this.  When she
wrote to Nettie she did not refer to Nettie's letter, "I just let it
pass."

27
The plaintiff denied that she had any
control over who was to be invited to Carol's wedding.  She knew that Nettie
wanted to attend the wedding.  She said that Nettie had taken Carol and Michael
out prior to the wedding; that when they came to Port Alberni for the wedding,
she phoned Nettie and was told by her that she was coming to the wedding.

28
Nettie never came to the farm to visit
them, although she was invited to do so according to the witness.  In 1990 the
plaintiff and her husband moved back to Port Alberni.  They had leased the farm
with an option to purchase to the lessee.  She knows that the defendant Stefan
Vatamaniuck took Nettie to the hospital on November 11, 1991.  She at first did
not visit Nettie because she had a cold.  After the first week she visited her
every afternoon, and she and her husband also went to see her in the evenings.
She says that Nettie would have a room full of visitors, and that she
"didn't want to see my husband."  Her husband then left, and she told
Nettie that she was leaving too and she left.

29
Counsel for the plaintiff led evidence of
what the plaintiff's father, Mr. Romaniuk, told her about her parents'
marriage, for some time prior to his death.  His position is that the evidence
is not hearsay; that it goes to the state of mind of her father at the time,
and is relevant to Nettie's expressed reason in her will for not leaving any
money to the plaintiff.  It bears on Nettie's interpretation as to what occurred
between her and the plaintiff.

30
It appeared clear as the case proceeded,
that both counsel wished to lead hearsay evidence with regard to various
matters which they submitted were relevant to the matters at issue.  Rather
than attempt to deal with each matter as it arose, I accepted counsels'
submission that the evidence should be heard, and the issue of admissibility
decided at a later date.

31
Having heard all of the evidence, I do
not propose to deal with the hearsay issue or evidence in any detail.  Anything
Nettie said or did, which has some bearing on her reasons for making the
disposition she made, and for not making any provision for the plaintiff, is
admissible under section 3 of the Act.  Under section 4 the only question is
that of the weight to be given to that evidence.  And in deciding what weight
to be given to it, the court must have regard "to all the circumstances
from which an inference may reasonably be drawn as to the accuracy or otherwise
of the statement."  Hence, it would seem to follow, although I need not
decide, that evidence other than what the deceased said or did, may be
admissible under these provisions as well.  The only restriction, if it may be
called that, on the court's discretion, is that the court must be satisfied
that the evidence is proper.

32
Other evidence was led, by both parties,
as to what was said by Nettie's first husband on particular occasions.  But
most of that evidence dealt with matters of common ground, and was established
by admissible evidence.  I refer, by way of example, to Mr. Romaniuk's
statements to the plaintiff and to her daughter, a year or so before his death,
that he couldn't take it anymore and wanted a divorce.  It is common ground
that he and Nettie were having marital problems for some time before his
death.  And in her July 11, 1989 letter Nettie explained the fact that in the
last year of his life Mr. Romaniuk was having mental problems as a result of
the hardening of his arteries.

33
Finally, on the question of hearsay, both
counsels submitted generally that hearsay in the case at bar should be
admissible pursuant to the principles laid down
in
Regina v. Smith
,

1992 CanLII 79 (SCC)
,
[1992] 2 S.C.R. 915
; that the evidence satisfied the criteria of necessity and
reliability.  I have concluded that I need not decide whether or not this is
so, in the circumstances of this case.  However, and while each case must
depend upon its facts, I question generally the application of such principles
when the evidence sought to be led is that of statements made by a deceased
person other than the testatrix, to the witness and beneficiary under the
will.  The person testifying would hardly be a disinterested person, and
reliability would be most difficult to determine.

34
The plaintiff testified that for some
time prior to his death, her father told her about marital problems he was
having with Nettie.  She said that Nettie called her father unkind names, and
said that he was "throwing his money around".  Her father had been
complaining to her "for a long time", but things were bad for about a
year prior to his death.  Her father told her that he wanted a divorce
"because he couldn't take it anymore."  She recalled a particular
incident when she was at work and Carol, then 14 years of age, was at home.
Her father had come to their home.  He was quite upset, and was complaining
that he wanted a divorce.  She had to go home and calm him down.  He suggested
to her that Nettie was drawing money out of the bank, and then accusing him of
doing it.  She does not know of any steps taken by either parent to obtain a
divorce.

35
The plaintiff gave fairly detailed
evidence that she and her husband have been operating the farm or ranch at a
loss.  As a result she has been working "off the farm" as a camp
attendant, to supplement their income.  The ranch is made up of two sections of
land.  They are attempting to purchase a third section from the government.
She said that in the past year income was approximately $35,000.00 while
expenses were approximately $40,000.00.  I will note here that in my view the
net worth statement, prepared by the plaintiff and her husband and put into
evidence, does not present a clear picture of the plaintiff's financial
circumstances.  Other expenses include substantial loans made on the farm, some
quite recently, to purchase cattle and to otherwise improve the farm.  They
raise cattle on the farm which are sold each year.  The value of the stock at
the time of the trial was $45,000.00.  The plaintiff's husband receives a
private pension of approximately $800.00 per month.  They are both 64.  When
they turn 65, and by now they have done so, they will both receive their Canada
Pension.  The plaintiff's health is good, although she has high blood pressure.

36
On cross-examination the plaintiff said
that she did not expect to receive any monies from the estate of her father,
Peter Romaniuk.  She had expected that he would leave everything to her mother,
and vice versa, which she felt would be "correct, right and just."
She acknowledged that after the funeral, she ascertained that save for the $4,000.00
in bonds, which she received, all of her father's assets had been transferred
to Nettie.  And she knew that Nettie had control of the assets because they had
been transferred to her prior to her father's death.  It was then put to the
witness that if that was the case, she had no good reason to say anything to
Nettie "since she already had everything".  Her response was that she
was only doing what she thought she should do as executrix.  She was asked
whether she meant by that, "getting assets for herself", and she said
no.

37
She was pressed as to why she had to say
anything to Nettie at all, about her father's bank accounts, if she was of the
view that Nettie should have all of his estate on his death.  She repeated that
she was only doing what she thought she should do, and that she was "not
trying to take anything from mother", adding that she didn't need, and
still doesn't need, the money.

38
She would not agree that, as indicated by
the statement of claim in that action, the net sum she sued Nettie for was
around $18,000.00.  She acknowledged that she did sue for a return of the car,
which had been transferred into Nettie's name when her father was in the
hospital.  It was put to her that since her mother already had the car, there
was no need for her to sue, and have it returned to the estate.  She denied
that she was trying to get the car for herself.  She said she sued to have the
car returned to the estate, so that she could probate the will.  She reiterated
that she did not want Nettie's money, her home or her car.

39
She was asked again, if it was still her
position that her mother should have recovered all of her father's estate, and
she said that it was.  She was asked again, why then did she have to sue Nettie
to get the car back.  My rough note of her answer is:

She said very mean
things about father.  I wanted her to apologize and she wouldn't.  Father was a
good man.  He worked hard and would not hurt anybody.

40
She then acknowledged that she knew that
the cheques had been signed by her father in the hospital; adding that he
didn't really sign them because a nurse had helped him.  It was put to her
again, that she did not have to sue her mother to have the monies returned to
the estate, because her mother already had the monies.  And she again denied
that she wanted the monies for herself.  The following question and answer was
then put and given with regard to the monies:

QIf
you didn't want it and your mother had it - you did not need to sue her to get
it, to give it to her - correct?

AYes.

41
She was then taken through her statement
of claim in the earlier action.  The gist of her evidence was that she did not
want the sums and chattels, such as the car, furniture, tools and so on, which
she claimed therein.  Again, she denied that she wanted damages from her
mother, although claims were advanced for damages in the action.

42
Counsel continued to press the witness,
that she had sued Nettie because she wanted the monies and chattels for
herself, and she continued to deny that such was the case.  She did not know
why her father left her anything.  She did not want anything from her mother.
She wanted Nettie to apologize for the things she had said about her father.
Finally, she said that she told Nettie that she didn't want to go to court, but
wanted her to apologize, and "tell the others" that her father was
not the ogre Nettie said he was.

43
The statement of claim, statement of
defence, counterclaim, and defence to counterclaim, in the action were then
referred to, and which speak for themselves.  It was noted that in her reply to
the statement of defence, she alleged that the larger bank account in the sum
of $27,854.95 was a common account, not a joint account.  Also in her defence
to Nettie's counterclaim, she pleaded that adequate provision had been made for
Nettie, and that she was "independently wealthy".

44
The plaintiff then had put to her
evidence she gave at the trial on direct examination.  There she gave the
following evidence with regard to the "missing assets":

QOkay,
and what attempts did you take to solve the question that
the assets weren't
what you expected them to be?
Did you discuss the matter with your mother?

AYes,
and she refused.

QRefused
to what?

A
She
refused to put everything back
.

And:

QOkay,
are you aware of the fact that your mother may have a claim under the
Testator's Family Maintenance Act?

AYes.

QAnd
you are proceeding with the action anyway?

AYes.

QAnd
why is that?

AWell,

for the simple reason that father had left me some money and the car and
it's not there
.

(My emphasis)

45
The plaintiff agreed that after the
lawsuit she and Nettie stopped seeing each other socially.  She said that it
was because Nettie was angry, but she was not.  She denied going out of her way
to make Nettie unwelcome at her home and with her children.

46
At the time of Carol's wedding, Carol and
her husband to be lived in Port Alberni, as did the plaintiff.  The wedding
took place in August of 1989.  Nettie did not attend.  She denied going out of
her way to see that Nettie did not get an invitation.  She left it to Carol to
send Nettie the invitation.  She was then referred to Nettie's letter dated
July 11th, wherein she states that Carol told her that they wanted Nettie and
her husband to attend the wedding, and that she, that is Nettie, should speak
to the plaintiff about it.  She was then asked if she knew why Nettie didn't
attend Carol's wedding and she said "no, I don't."  She gave the same
answer when she was asked why Nettie didn't attend her son's wedding reception
which was held in Port Alberni.  She had heard that Nettie had watched either
the wedding or the reception from across the street.

47
She denied that she asked her parents for
a $40,000.00 loan when they purchased the farm.  They paid for the farm by
selling their house and five acres which they had at the time.  They also
borrowed approximately $35,000.00 from a credit union.

48
She did not visit with her mother after
the lawsuit.  When they left the farm and moved back to Port Alberni for two
years, she still did not visit her mother.  She says that she telephoned her
"without success"; that she saw Nettie in stores "once in
awhile" and that "that was it."  She never took Nettie out to
dinner.  She never went over to see Nettie, to see if she needed anything or
any help.  She did not see if her children, the grandchildren, were visiting
Nettie, because "that was their concern not mine".  She did not
attend the wedding when Nettie married Mr. Richardson, and she did not send
them a gift.

49
She knew that Nettie was getting on, and
had a heart condition.  She did not know that she had cancer until around the
time that she went into the hospital.  Stefan Vatamaniuck came to her house to
tell her.  He told her that it was unlikely that she would live very long, and
that she should go and see her and make  amends.  She didn't go at first
because she had a cold.  When she finally visited Nettie she was sleeping.
Nettie's husband George was in the next bed, and appeared to be "very
irate".  She didn't know why.  He then started saying mean things to her
so she walked out.  When asked what George said to her, she said that at the
time he was talking to Joseph and Toots Schultz, but she heard him say the word
"court".

50
She agreed that her husband went with her
on the first occasion when she went to visit Nettie.  She also agreed that
Nettie told them to leave saying, "yes, she did not want to see him",
referring to her husband.  She then said that Nettie told her to stay, but that
George would have to leave.  She then left because her husband left.

51
The witness insists that after the trial
she and Nettie reconciled.  She said that Nettie wrote the letter to her and
said she was sorry.  She wrote back and said everything was forgotten, to
forget about it.  She could not be sure whether the letter she referred to was
the one dated July 11th in evidence.  She read it again, and then said no that
was not the letter, because that letter was written after she had written to
Nettie.  She assumes that she wrote it about two weeks before Nettie wrote her
letter.  It was pointed out to her that Nettie did not acknowledge her letter
in her letter.  She then said that Nettie had written another letter to her
husband George, in which she apologized to him.  I did not believe the
witness.  I am satisfied on the whole of the evidence that Nettie and the
plaintiff never did reconcile, that letters, other than the two in evidence and
to which I have referred, were not exchanged between them, and that Nettie was
prevented from going to Carol's wedding; that all of this was the plaintiff's
doing, not Nettie's.  I find the plaintiff's evidence in these and other areas
simply to be too inconsistent and improbable, in light of other evidence and
probabilities, and even her own conduct over the years.

52
She then had put to her testimony given
by Nettie at the previous trial to the effect that while they lived in
Saskatchewan her father had been unemployed for most of 10 years, while Nettie
worked most of the time.  She then had portions of Nettie's July 11th letter
read to her.  She denied that her father went to her, that is to the plaintiff,
"when things went wrong."  She said that he did not come to her until
the latter part of his life.  She also denied that she ever sided with her
father.

53
On redirect examination she said again
that she and Nettie had reconciled.  She said that they wrote back and forth
about three times a year; that it was in her July 11th letter that Nettie first
spoke of the problems between the two of them.  In this regard she could not
explain why Nettie continued to say in her letters that they should bury the
hatchet.  She believes that there were four or five letters written after the
July 11th letter.  She wrote to her mother first and told her that she was
sorry.  Nettie wrote to her telling her that she was sorry.  Those letters are
not in evidence.  And it will be seen that I have had trouble with the
plaintiff's evidence in a number of areas, and this is one of them.  I find it
difficult to believe that Nettie would be writing letters after the July 11th
letter, given the fact that Carol's wedding took place in the following month,
and which to her sorrow the plaintiff would not let her attend.  And I am
satisfied that Nettie and the plaintiff never did reconcile, notwithstanding
Nettie's attempts to do so.

54
Nettie's granddaughter Carol, now Carol
Bye, testified that she lived in Port Alberni, save for a few years when she
lived in Fort St. John when she was around 15 years of age.  She is 31 years of
age, married to Michael, and they have one child.  She remembers her
grandparents through personal contact with them.  She used to visit them, and
they came to visit at times.

55
She was never aware of any problems
between her grandparents, until an occasion when she was 13 to 15 years of age
and her grandfather came to their home.  She was sick and was home from
school.  Her grandfather arrived at the door and seemed to be very shaken up.
He told her that he and her grandmother were getting divorced.  She phoned her
mother to come home and calm him down.

56
She knew that her mother and Nettie were
involved in a dispute over her grandfather's estate.  Her mother didn't talk to
her about it, until she showed her a transcript of the evidence given at the
trial.  However, after returning to Port Alberni to live in 1981 she did go and
visit Nettie on occasion.  And when she became engaged, she and Michael visited
Nettie and told her about the engagement.  Nettie and her husband George took
them out for a congratulatory dinner, and also gave them a gift of $500.00 in
cash.  She says she told Nettie at the time that she would like to have her at
the wedding.

57
Nettie did not come to her wedding.
Written invitations were sent out.  She couldn't remember whether she sent the
invitation to Nettie, or whether her mother did.  She cannot explain why Nettie
did not come to her wedding.  She's not sure whether she saw Nettie after the
wedding.  She said that she might have come into the store where she was
working, "that was it."  She couldn't explain why post-wedding
contact with Nettie was "minimal".

58
On cross-examination Ms. Bye acknowledged
that at the time of her engagement she lived approximately three blocks from
the home of Stefan Vatamaniuck and his wife.  She used to walk her dog past
their home on occasion, and she would chat with them.  She was referred to a specific
day when she talked with Mr. and Mrs. Vatamaniuck, and she was asked whether
she had any conversation with them with regard to whether or not an invitation
was going to be given to Nettie.  She said "no, I don't believe so."
She denied telling them that since her parents were paying for part of her
wedding, they had some say in who was to be invited.  She denied telling them
that she could not invite her parents and Nettie at the same time, calling it
"an absolute lie".

59
She was then asked whether, when Nettie
took her and Michael to dinner, she told Nettie to speak to the plaintiff about
her invitation to the wedding.  Her answer again was "no, I don't believe
so."  She was then referred to Nettie's letter dated July 11th to her
mother, which she had not seen before.  It is stated in this letter that the
witness had told Nettie that she would have to speak to the plaintiff about
Nettie going to her wedding.  She was then asked if that was an accurate
statement by her grandmother.  She said that she didn't know, that "I
don't know what she thought I meant by that."  She would not agree that
Nettie took it to mean that she had to ask the plaintiff for permission to go
to her wedding, saying "no, it was up to me."  It will be seen that I
have concluded that while Ms. Bye and her husband to be may have wanted Nettie
to come to the wedding, Nettie was required to obtain permission from the
plaintiff before doing so; and that permission was never given.  I reject the
plaintiff's evidence, as well as that of Ms. Bye, to the effect that they have
no idea why Nettie did not attend the wedding.

60
I did not find the evidence of Susan
Gieni, the 35 year old wife of Greg Gieni, to be of assistance.  I now turn to
the evidence of the plaintiff's husband, George Gieni.  He is 64 years of age.
He is a farmer and a heavy equipment operator.  He got along with his
father-in-law, Peter Romaniuk.  Each helped the other build his family home.
Initially, he also got along with Nettie quite well, and often went fishing
with her in her boat.  He believes he had a normal relationship with her up
until the time of Peter Romaniuk's funeral.  The plaintiff had received a
letter from a lawyer advising her that she was the executrix of her father's
estate.  They went to tell Nettie this, and she said "I'll fight
it".  He says he did not understand what she meant, and that he and his
wife did not understand what an executrix was.

61
Counsel then put to him the following
evidence given by Nettie during the trial:

274  QNow,
when your daughter -- just -- what happened between you and your daughter after
your husband died?  Did she come to see you?

AShe
came but my daughter did not say much.  It was my son-in-law.

275  QThey both came together?

AThey came together, but my son-in-law came
when I had company.

276  QYes?

AAnd
he came and in a very hostile way.

277  QWhat

AHe

mean, penniless?"  He says, "Well, he has nothing, no money in the

278  QYes?

AWell,
then he attacked me with that.

do you mean, "attacked" you?

He said that he and the plaintiff did
go down to see Nettie, but only to inform her that the plaintiff was the

62
Mr. Gieni said that he never had any
discussions with Nettie about what he called the "missing money".
However, he did recall her saying, just before the funeral, in the presence of
the family, that Mr. Romaniuk had been doing strange things, i.e. going to the
bank and taking money out, and then giving it away to people on the street.
When asked what he thought about that he said that it was possible.

63
The witness then described how they
loaned $35,000.00 to a friend to buy the cattle farm, and how they had to take
it over when the loan was not repaid.  According to him they have been trying
to sell the farm since 1982, but without success.  They did sell it to a young
couple in the spring of 1990, and they then moved back to Port Alberni for two
years.  However, they eventually had to take the farm back.

64
Mr. Gieni denies that he and his wife
ever attempted to borrow $40,000.00 from Nettie in order to purchase the farm.
He has no idea why Nettie would suggest that they did.  He was present in the
courtroom during the first trial, but he did not give evidence.

65
He agreed that after the trial he and the
plaintiff had very little contact with Nettie, since they were living up
country.  They had some contact by letter, and his wife did the writing.  They
were only able to find the two letters which they have produced.  He believes
the first letter from Nettie arrived shortly after the court case; that it was
in that letter that she said "let's bury the hatchet", and they wrote
back saying "no problem".  This was "about 1981".  He
"felt pleased because she apologized to me."  Clearly the witness is
mistaken.  There was no contact between the plaintiff and Nettie for many years
after the trial.  Nettie's letter in which she apologized to the plaintiff's
husband was sent on July 11, 1989, approximately one month before Carol's
wedding.  She also requested permission from the plaintiff to go to the wedding
at that time.  If they had reconciled in 1981 as suggested by the witness,
there would have been no reason to apologize or to make the request.

66
He does not know why Nettie did not come
to Carol's wedding.  They came down to Port Alberni again in the spring of
1990.  They met Nettie and her second husband on the street.  He did not notice
any animosity at that time.  They did not visit her at her home prior to
entering hospital.  He confirmed that when they went to see her, Nettie told
him that she didn't want to see him.  He has no explanation for this.

67
I do not propose to deal in any detail
with the net worth statement produced by the plaintiff and her husband.  Some
of the values put forth seem to be questionable.  The records show that they
borrowed $60,000.00 in 1993 for farm purposes.  They paid $28,000.00 of that
money back in the year 1994 from revenues.  He says that they lose money operating
the ranch, but they have no other choice.  He presently receives a monthly
cheque of about $870.00.  By now he and his wife are both 65 and will be
receiving their Canada Pension.  His evidence, like that of the plaintiff,
suggests that they are in dire financial straits.  However, I am not prepared
to find that that is the case on the evidence before me.  In addition to the
ranch, which produces a substantial income, most of which is taken up to repay
farm loans, and the value of the ranch, the plaintiff and her husband jointly
must be receiving approximately $2,500.00 per month income by way of pension.
In my opinion the plaintiff is not in need in the circumstances of this case.

68
On cross-examination the witness said
that he and the plaintiff only saw Nettie once from the time of Peter
Romaniuk's funeral to the trial in April of 1988.  On that occasion, in 1978,
they thought that it would be "nice to go and see how she is".  When
they arrived at her door Nettie appeared with her second husband, and she told
them that she did not want to speak with them.  The witness is mistaken as to
the date, or as to the presence of Mr. Richardson, because Nettie did not
remarry until April 24, 1981.

69
He then had read to him the evidence
given by Nettie at the trial, and which was put to the plaintiff earlier, in
which she describes his "hostile" visit to her home.  He then had
this further evidence read to him:

281  QDid
she speak to you?

ANo.

282  QYou
weren't ignoring her or anything?

she came but it was her husband that spoke to me.

283  QAnd

284  QAnd

at that time?

AI

285  QDid

286  QWhat
was that?

AHe
