287  QI
see.  Anything else?

AWell,
then they left.

70
He was present during the trial and had
heard Nettie testify.  However, he and his wife apparently have poor memories,
and that is why they ordered a transcript of the trial.  He did not agree with
much of the assertions made by Nettie in the passages quoted.  He said that he
did not speak to Nettie at all on the occasion of their visit; that it was the
plaintiff who did the talking.  It was put to him that he would have heard her
testimony at the trial, and that it would have "stood out".  He
acknowledged that he probably heard it, but he couldn't remember. Again he said
that his memory wasn't that good.

71
Mr. Gieni was asked whether he discussed
with the plaintiff whether she should sue Nettie.  He said "we never
realized we were suing her."  The plaintiff did not tell him that she was
suing Nettie for $18,000.00.  She did tell him that her lawyer told her that
the two cheques had been "improperly signed."  He was asked whether
he and his wife ever discussed "who should have Peter's property" and
he said "we had no claim, she was his wife."  He agreed that Nettie
"deserved" her husband's estate.  He did not understand that the
lawsuit was designed to recover property and money which would go to the
plaintiff.  His evidence, like that of the plaintiff, with regard to the prior
action is most difficult to accept, given other evidence including the
pleadings, and the evidence given by the plaintiff, in that action.

72
The defendant Stefan Vatamaniuck
testified that he is the 56 year old nephew of Nettie, one of the executors of
her estate, and a beneficiary.  His mother is the defendant Virginia Ekdahl,
Nettie's sister.  He is a retired RCMP officer.  He started his career in 1958
in Port Alberni, and over the years was transferred to Campbell River, the
Queen Charlottes, Dawson Creek, and other locations, until his retirement in
1991.  He retired as a result of two serious brain operations, after which he
had to learn to walk and talk again.

73
He has always been friends with Nettie.
He lived with her in her home for two years in Port Alberni.  His wife's family
has always lived in Port Alberni.  Hence, they returned to Port Alberni on many
occasions to visit relatives and so on.  On those trips he would have a visit
with Nettie.  She never told him about any problems she and her husband Peter
were having.  He knew the plaintiff.  He remembers coming home to Port Alberni
for holidays, and being told about the court case between the plaintiff and
Nettie.  He said that after that their relationship deteriorated rapidly, and
they were not on speaking terms.

74
Nettie did not tell him what happened.
The only thing she told him was, that she recovered the whole of Peter's
estate.  When Nettie became ill with cancer in November of 1991, she gave him a
power of attorney "in case anything happens".  She did not give him
any specific instructions as to how it was to be used.

75
The witness recalled how he and his wife
had a conversation with Carol Bye shortly before her marriage, when she was
walking her dog past their home.  He and his wife were working in the flower
garden.  During the conversation the matter of Carol's wedding came up.  He
says that she mentioned that she would have liked to have had Nettie come to
the wedding; that because her parents were paying for a part of her wedding she
had to choose between them and Nettie.  She did not tell them why, but he says
he knew that the plaintiff and Nettie were not speaking.  He was told later by
Nettie that she was not invited to the wedding.

76
On cross-examination he said that he and
his wife moved back to Port Alberni in 1987.  Prior to then he and his wife
were only in Port Alberni when they were on holidays.  On those occasions he
would drop in and see Nettie, have lunch with her and so on.  During those
visits he learned about the results of the court case, and that Nettie and the
plaintiff were no longer speaking.  It was his understanding that there was no
communication between Nettie and the plaintiff in the 1980s, after the court
case.  He was not aware of the letter evidence, until he heard about in these
proceedings.  He was then directed to read the letter, and asked whether, in
light of what Nettie had told him, he was surprised to learn that there was
"frequent communication by letter between the plaintiff and Nettie".
He said that he would find it very surprising, and just as surprising if there
had been a number of phone calls between them.  Nettie did not tell him about
the two letters, or about any other letters or telephone conversations with the
plaintiff.

77
He describes Nettie as a strong willed
woman.  During the last two weeks of her life in the hospital, while she was
immobile, and sedated with Gravol, she was very lucid.  She couldn't hold her
food down.  She declined to take morphine if her pain became intense.  She was
the sort of woman who believed strongly in things, and stuck to her position.

78
He agreed that Carol Bye regularly walked
her dog past their home during the material time.  On occasion she would come
in for tea.  He recalled that she was in her twenties at the time, and that the
wedding was in August of 1989.  When asked about her testimony, wherein she
denied discussing with him and his wife Nettie coming to the wedding, he said
that she either had a very short memory or was a liar.  I accept this witness's
evidence, and that of his wife to which I will refer in a moment, that Ms. Bye
did tell them in effect that Nettie could not come to the wedding because of
the plaintiff.  Ms. Bye is mistaken.  Nettie's evidence, as contained in her
letter, is to the same effect, that is that Ms. Bye told her that it was up to
the plaintiff whether or not Nettie could go to the wedding.

79
Mr. Vatamaniuck said that when Ms. Bye
would visit them, she would often discuss how her life was going, her future
husband, her residence, her job and so on.  However, she did not tell him about
her dinner with Nettie, or the gift she gave them.  His knowledge as to why
Nettie did not go to the wedding came from Nettie.  He did not discuss it with
the plaintiff or her husband.  The falling out occurred as a result of the
court case.  She never gave him any details, or any other reasons.

80
It was put to the witness that when he
returned to Port Alberni in 1987 Nettie's attitude toward the plaintiff was
quite strong.  He did not agree.  My rough note of his answer, referring to
Nettie, is as follows:

She was always trying to
get in touch with her daughter and grandchildren - to patch things up.  I guess
with regard to the court case.  This is what she told me.  Her grandchildren
had been alienated.

81
He was asked whether Nettie ever told him
that she did not want the plaintiff to go near her house.  He said "yes,
in the hospital."  From that point on she said on many occasions, that
neither the plaintiff nor her husband was to be allowed into her home; that
they were not to get anything, "not even a string".  He acknowledged
that earlier Nettie had been trying to reconcile with the plaintiff.  He said
"she was making attempts, but the plaintiff would have nothing to do with
her"; that Nettie was "very upset and hurt by it."

82
The witness and his mother visited Nettie
in the hospital every day.  He continued to do so by himself, when his mother
returned to Sechelt for a brief period.  He was present when the plaintiff and
her husband George came to the hospital to see Nettie.  He said that Nettie
told them that she did not want to see George.  George then said that he was
leaving and did so.  The plaintiff then said that if he was going she was going
too, and she left.

83
He saw the plaintiff on one other
occasion in the hospital.  He met her at the elevator or in the hall.  He was
on the way to visit Nettie.  He believes he asked the plaintiff how Nettie was
doing.  By then a sign had been placed on Nettie's door, that visitors had to
check at the front desk before entering the room.  He asked George Richardson,
who was staying in the room with Nettie, what the sign was all about.  He told
him that the plaintiff had come for a visit and had upset Nettie, that the sign
was to keep the plaintiff out.  He, the witness, had gone to tell the plaintiff
that Nettie was in the hospital, against Nettie's wishes.  When he told the
plaintiff that Nettie had terminal cancer she said that she would go and see
her.

84
The witness says that he and his wife
have clear title to their house which has been valued at $80,000.00 or
$90,000.00 but which they feel is worth $100,000.00 to $130,000.00.  He has a
monthly pension of $2,100.99.  He has bonds worth $5,000.00 or $6,000.00 about
to come due, and an RRSP having a value of around $25,000.00.

85
Finally the witness confirmed that Nettie
was not at Carol's wedding.  He and his wife received a written invitation to
the wedding, which required a reply.  He believes that Carol brought the
invitation to them personally.

86
Stefan Vatamaniuck's wife, 54 year old
Judy Vatamaniuck, also testified on behalf of the defendants.  She confirmed
that during the chance meeting with Carol Bye, when she was walking her dog,
Carol told her and her husband that because her mother was paying for part of
the wedding, and Nettie was not, Nettie was not coming.

87
She and her husband often visited
Nettie.  She knew from discussions with Nettie that there was "great
unhappiness there" with regard to the plaintiff; that Nettie was sad
because there was no hope of reconciliation.  Nettie did not tell her of her
efforts to reconcile with the plaintiff.  She was not Nettie's confidant.  She
said that Nettie and her husband always got along very well.  He visited her every
day at the hospital, and sat with her when she died.

88
She thought that she and Carol were
friends at the time.  She would drop in for tea and so on.  But she was not a
confidant.  She and her husband were invited to and went to Carol's wedding.
She did not know that Carol was now denying that the conversation took place
with her and her husband.  When asked whether it was possible that her memory
was foggy, she said that she couldn't recall all that was discussed, but she did
remember that that was said, i.e. that because the plaintiff was paying for
part of the wedding, and Nettie was not, Nettie could not come to the wedding.

89
Emmaline Jesse Schultz testified that she
is 62 years of age, and that she and her husband lived a few doors away from
Nettie.  They knew her for about 10 years.  They also knew George Richardson.
She described them as "our adopted parents".  They cut the grass for
them, and did what inside work was needed, over the 10 year period.  They were
very good friends.

90
She was asked whether Nettie ever
discussed with her her relationship with the plaintiff.  She said that she
did.  My rough note of her answer was:

She said she really
loved her, and would love to have had her around, but her daughter did not see
fit to love her, and there was a lot of friction between them.

She never saw the plaintiff or her
husband visiting Nettie, or at her house.  She was asked whether Nettie ever
explained why there was friction between them.  She said that it was "over
her husband's will", and "also they wanted to borrow money off her
and she didn't loan it to them."

91
The witness said that when she first met
Nettie there didn't seem to be any problem with the grandchildren.  This
changed later, around the time of Carol's wedding.  She remembers Nettie
crying, and saying that she was told that she couldn't go to the wedding.

92
In November of 1991 when Nettie became
ill she and her husband took her to the emergency.  The doctors told them that
Nettie had cancer.  They visited her in the hospital.  At the time Nettie's
husband was in a different part of the hospital, and at his request he was
moved into the same room as Nettie.

93
They observed that Nettie had many
visitors when they visited her.  They were there on one occasion when the
plaintiff visited.  When they walked in the door they saw the plaintiff
standing over Nettie crying.  Nettie was unconscious.  She heard Nettie's
husband say to get that woman out of there, that Nettie didn't want her there,
that she had caused Nettie enough pain.  And he was crying.  She heard the
plaintiff say "this is my mom, you are not my mom."  The witness and
her husband then departed.

94
On cross-examination Ms. Schultz
acknowledged that she would be surprised if she were told that during the
period in question, 1981 to 1991, letters were written back and forth between
the plaintiff and Nettie.  She was then shown Nettie's letter dated July 11th,
and portions of it were read to her.  She was then asked whether Nettie ever
told her about anything that she thought she did which was wrong, i.e. between
her and the plaintiff.  The witness said no.  With regard to the hospital
incident, it occurred at a time when Nettie was unconscious "a lot of the
time".  There was no one else in the room but Nettie, her husband George,
and the plaintiff.  Nettie was unconscious, and her husband and the plaintiff
were crying.

95
The plaintiff was called to the stand, by
consent, to give rebuttal evidence with regard to the hospital incident.  She
said that it was her last meeting with Nettie.  She kissed her, but she was not
responding, i.e. she was unconscious.  Then Mr. and Mrs. Schultz came in.
Nettie's husband George started yelling "saying I tried to take everything
away from mother and that he wanted me out of there."  She said she never
spoke one word to Mr. and Mrs. Schultz or to Nettie's husband.

96
Virginia Ekdahl testified that she was
Nettie's sister.  There were 13 children in the family.  Two sisters and one
brother are still alive.  She is 78 years of age and now lives in Sechelt.  She
has been widowed for about 11 years.  She has always kept in touch with
Nettie.  They would visit back and forth.  Nettie would also visit their other
sister, Stefan Vatamaniuck's mother, in Saskatchewan, fairly frequently.

97
There is no doubt, according to this
witness, that Nettie and Peter Romaniuk were having problems prior to his
death.  Nettie complained to her that Peter Romaniuk was very hard to get along
with, and that she couldn't take it anymore.  She described one incident
related to her by Nettie.  Nettie had been visiting in Saskatchewan for about a
month.  When she came home she received a telephone call from a legal secretary
with regard to Peter's will.  She went down to their safety deposit box in the
bank, and found that Peter's will was missing.  She then confronted him about
this in Woodward's store, where an argument commenced and ended at their home.
Nettie said in effect that the plaintiff and her husband had persuaded Peter to
change his will by leaving everything to the plaintiff.  As a result Nettie
refused to cook for Peter, because she was "no longer his wife
anyway".  In the end it was the witness's understanding from Nettie, that
Peter did not change his will, but left everything to Nettie.  However, we know
that in fact he did change it.

98
Mrs. Ekdahl also said that both Nettie
and Peter told her that the plaintiff and her husband had attempted to borrow
$40,000.00 from them, "when they were going to move to Fort St. John to
buy the ranch."  Nettie said that they told the plaintiff and her husband
that they didn't have $40,000.00 to lend them.  After that, according to the witness,
Nettie and the plaintiff never got along.  Nettie believed that the plaintiff
taught her children not to communicate with or speak to Nettie.  Only David
would come to see her.  When she saw her other grandchildren on the street they
would turn and walk away.  In this regard, the witness described an incident
where she and Nettie were in a store when the plaintiff came in.  The plaintiff
came over to say hello to the witness.  Nettie then said hello to the
plaintiff, and the plaintiff turned and walked away.  Nettie tried to get in
touch with the plaintiff, but the plaintiff wouldn't have anything to do with
her.

99
Nettie also believed that the plaintiff's
husband, George, coerced the plaintiff into having her father, Peter, change
the will in her favour; that Peter was told that if something happened to him,
mother (Nettie) "would get together with some other man and spend all his
money."  Peter was thus talked into leaving everything to the plaintiff.

100
With regard to Carol's wedding, Mrs.
Ekdahl said that Nettie "wanted so badly to go" that she phoned Carol
and invited her and her future husband to go out for dinner.  After dinner she
brought them to her home and gave them the $500.00 gift.  Carol told her at
that time that she would really like her to come to the wedding, but that she
had to speak to the plaintiff.  She later phoned Nettie and said that she was
sorry that she could not come to the wedding, because the plaintiff did not
want her at the wedding.

101
Nettie was embarrassed because she could
not go to the wedding, so she arranged to visit her sister in Saskatoon at the
time of the wedding.  On another occasion, when one of her grandchildren was
married, Nettie went down to the church and stood outside crying while she
watched guests and the participants come and go from the church.

102
Nettie only told Mrs. Ekdahl's son Stefan
that she was dying of cancer.  The witness did not find this out until she
arrived at the hospital.  She stayed with Stefan, and they visited Nettie in
the hospital for approximately 10 days.  She then had to return home to Sechelt
to take care of some business.  Nettie died before she could return.

103
She was there when the plaintiff and her
husband George came into Nettie's room.  She said that Nettie was upset, saying
"I don't want to see George."  The plaintiff and George then went to
the foot of Nettie's bed.  Nettie asked George "what are you doing
here" and he said "I came to see you".  Nettie said "I
don't want to see you".  Kay then said "if you don't want to see
George, I am leaving too", and she left.  She did not see the plaintiff at
the hospital again.  However, Nettie told her that she did come to visit her
again, and that the plaintiff started to argue with her "about old
times".  Nettie was crying when she related this to the witness, and said
"if Kay would only come and put her arms around me."  Nettie also
told her "please don't let Kay have my home or anything in it, not one
string".

104
The defendant Stefan Vatamaniuck made all
the funeral arrangements.  The plaintiff came to the funeral, but she did not
sit with members of the family.  The plaintiff did not come to Nettie's home
before or after the funeral.

105
On cross-examination, the plaintiff said
again that she had regular contact with Nettie, even when she was married to
Peter Romaniuk.  My rough note of her evidence with regard to Mr. Romaniuk is
as follows:

Peter was a very
disturbed person.  He never had a friend or neighbour.  He didn't trust
anybody, even the banks, "everyone was a crook".  He never showed
Nettie any affection.  She would say to him "Peter, why can't I give you a
kiss", and he would say "Go away".  She would say "Don't
you love me?", and he would say "Didn't I marry you?".

She, the witness, did not dislike Mr.
Romaniuk and she got along with him, but she did not like the way that he
treated Nettie.

106
She was questioned with regard to the
$40,000.00 loan.  She is aware that the plaintiff and her husband deny ever
asking for the money.  She said that Nettie told her that the plaintiff and her
husband George were very angry when they were turned down; that they believed
that Nettie had persuaded Peter not to loan them the money.  They wanted the money
to buy the ranch and to put cattle on it.  Nettie was upset about the matter.
She and the plaintiff never got along very well after that.

107
She was asked to reiterate the incidents
which occurred, after Nettie returned from Saskatchewan and received a
telephone call with regard to her husband's will.  Nettie told her that at the
time she thought that "the secretary was trying to tell me
something."  She immediately went to the bank and found that her husband's
will was not in the safety deposit box.  She then went to a nearby Woodward's
store and confronted Mr. Romaniuk.  They then went home and had a "big
fight".  Nettie blamed the plaintiff for what had happened, and refused to
be Mr. Romaniuk's wife any further.  Apparently she stopped cooking for him and
so on until she was told by him that a new will leaving his estate to her had
been made.  She did not tell the witness that she had seen that will.

108
With regard to the plaintiff's influence,
the witness said that Nettie told her that she believed that the plaintiff
influenced her father to do what he did.  She was "sure they got after
him" referring to the plaintiff and her husband George.  The witness said
that she could not recall whether Nettie thought that, or whether her husband
Peter had told her that that was the case.

109
Mrs. Ekdahl denied that, to her knowledge,
Nettie confided in the plaintiff with regard to her marital problems, or that
she confided with her, the witness, in that regard.  Nettie never gave her
details of the marital problems.  She just said "you don't know what goes
on behind closed doors"; that she had a "horrible life which we
didn't know about."

110
She was then referred to Nettie's letter
to the plaintiff dated July 11th.  She described the letter as a "begging
letter", saying that in effect Nettie was "begging to be asked to
Carol's wedding."  When it was pointed out that she was apologizing to
George, she said "all because she wanted to be invited to the
wedding."  When it was suggested to her that Nettie could have gone to the
wedding, and that Carol had testified that she had invited her, the witness
simply replied "I believe my sister."  Nettie told her that Carol
told her that the plaintiff did not want her at the wedding.  When asked
whether Carol was lying she again said "I believe my sister".

111
The witness was asked whether she thought
that Nettie's dying wish that the plaintiff not have her home, or anything in
it, was a rational wish.  My note of her answer is:

She meant it - from what
went on before - she did not mention what she was going to do.  She did not
mention Steve or I in there.  If she said she wanted to leave something to me
or otherwise, I would have called Steve to confirm it.

112
Mrs. Ekdahl lives alone in her home in
Sechelt.  Her home, which is clear title, has a value of approximately
$100,000.00.  She receives a monthly pension of $900.00 and has approximately
$60,000.00 in savings.  She saves her money because "I may get sick, I
don't want to rely on my children."  She has a son who lives in Vancouver
and a daughter who lives in San Diego.

113
The following are the agreed admissions in
this case.

(1)Concerning
the last will and testament of Peter Romaniuk (first husband of the testatrix)
the solicitor who drew the will has no recollection of the plaintiff or her
husband being present or involved in any other way with respect to receipt of
instructions.

(2)Concerning
preparation of the subject last will and testament the solicitor who drew the
will:

(a)was
not told of any reasons for disinheriting the plaintiff other than as expressed
in the will,

(b)was
not told of any reasons for disinheriting the grandchildren.

SUBMISSIONS

114
Counsel for the plaintiff made the
following submissions:  Nettie did not discharge her moral duty to the
plaintiff to make adequate provision for her proper maintenance and support.
The beneficiaries have no rights under the Act, and are in fact strangers to
it.  Those who do not qualify under the Act are not entitled to the same
consideration as those that do.

115
The only express reason given by Nettie
for not providing for the plaintiff is contained in paragraph 5 of her will,
"because she attempted to deny my inheritance following the death of my
first husband."  The will was made five weeks before her death.  That is
the only surrounding circumstance.

116
The other reasons given are those which
Nettie told the defendants.  The plaintiff and her husband coerced Mr. Romaniuk
into making a new will out in favour of the plaintiff.  He left everything to
the plaintiff in his will dated July 12, 1973.  He did not change the will back
to Nettie, "although she thought he had."

117
The evidence surrounding Nettie finding
out that her husband was changing his will is important.  She refused to cook
for her husband unless he changed his will and made her the beneficiary.  She
understood that the situation had been remedied.  She would have been very,
very upset when she learned that this was not the case, that the residue of his
estate was to go to the plaintiff.  All of her concerns and uncertainties then
were transferred to the plaintiff.  This was a crucial happening.

118
I pause here to note that most of the
assets had been signed over to Nettie by Mr. Romaniuk prior to his death; that
there is no evidence that Nettie knew that the plaintiff was the residual
beneficiary in Mr. Romaniuk's will until after his death.  The evidence is to
the contrary.

119
As to the plaintiff's action against
Nettie, her counsel agreed with the position of defence counsel that the action
simply does not make sense.  Counsel emphasized that the court is "dealing
with people who don't understand the basics."  The action was simply an
attempt to undo what Mr. Romaniuk had done prior to his death, that is the
signing of the two cheques and the transferring of property, such as the car,
to Nettie.  It will be seen that I do not agree with this submission.  There is
other evidence, including the provisions of the pleadings in that action, and
the plaintiff's evidence at the trial, which satisfies me that the plaintiff
was attempting to get what she considered to be her father's assets, and which
probably included the home which she referred to as her "father's
home".

120
Returning to counsel's submission he noted
that at least in the early years the relationship between Nettie, the
plaintiff, and her husband was normal.  The exception, according to Mrs.
Ekdahl, was the attempt by the plaintiff and her husband to borrow $40,000.00
from Nettie and her husband so that they could buy the ranch.  Her evidence was
that the relationship soured after that.  The court is left to decide whether
Nettie's "reasons were reasonable and rational".

121
Another reason asserted is that the
plaintiff and her husband influenced Peter Romaniuk to change his will.  The
plaintiff and her husband deny that they did so.  They are not sophisticated
people.  The statements attributed to Nettie have been distorted by the breakdown
of her marriage to Peter Romaniuk.  Nettie told Mrs. Ekdahl that there were
problems, but wouldn't give details.  Carol Bye testified about the time that
Peter Romaniuk came to her home and talked about those problems.  Obviously
Peter Romaniuk had problems.  And he went to his daughter, the plaintiff.
Nettie probably went to her sisters.  This is not the case of a daughter trying
to steal her mother's inheritance.  It is a case of the daughter undoing a
wrong, and vindicating her father's name.

122
The plaintiff was left with the mess
created by her father.  All of the parties wish that he had not left his estate
to his daughter.  There is really no evidence of the plaintiff and her husband
having anything to do with the making of Peter Romaniuk's will.  There is only
one reason given in the will by Nettie.  The rest are manufactured
afterthoughts.

123
Counsel submitted that there was no
evidence of any souring of Nettie's relationship with her grandchildren until
August of 1989 when Carol's marriage took place.  Carol's evidence was that she
was in no way dependent upon her mother as to who should come to her wedding.
I have already found that this is not the case; that everyone knew that Nettie
was dying to go to the wedding, and why she didn't go, i.e. the plaintiff would
not allow it.

124
Counsel relies on a recent Court of Appeal
decision in
Bell v. Roy Estate
,
1993 CanLII 1262 (BC CA)
,
[1993] 4 W.W.R. 40
, wherein the
headnote reads:

Under s. 2(4) of the
Act, the weight to be given to evidence of the
reasons
for disinheriting
a relative
is affected by its accuracy and not by morally acceptable or
unacceptable content.  The actual intentions of the maker of the will are to be
given an effect
which is largely denied by those authorities which place
reliance upon the notionally objective reasonable testator.  The trial judge
did not err in finding that the
burden was on the plaintiff to show that the
reasons acted upon by the testatrix were false or unwarranted
.  That burden
was not discharged.

(My emphasis)

125
In the case at bar, says counsel, no
adequate provision was made for the plaintiff, and she is in need, and that
should end the matter.  Alternatively, the court should only look at the reason
expressed in the will, and as to that reason Nettie was not warranted in her
belief that the plaintiff had attempted to deny her inheritance following the
death of her first husband.  The plaintiff and her husband wish to reside in
Port Alberni.  They should be given two-thirds of Nettie's estate.

126
I turn now to counsel's written
submissions.  I had asked both counsel to provide me with submissions on the
question of admissibility of some of the evidence.  I do not recall requesting
counsel to provide me with written submissions re-arguing their respective
cases.  However, both have done so.

127
Counsel's written submission is basically
the same as his oral submission.  And I will only refer to it briefly.  Under
the topic "The Major Issues at Trial" counsel refers to
Bell

and says:

So that the first point
that must be made is that the new emphasis being placed upon a testator's
reasons does not have the effect of superseding the traditional judicial
concern of addressing the issue of need of the applicant.

He then goes on to deal with his
second point that the beneficiaries, who are not applicants under the Act,
should be given secondary and not primary consideration, in determining whether
Nettie has appropriately dealt with any moral duty owed to the plaintiff.  He
says:

So that for example in
considering whether the testatrix in this case owes the plaintiff a moral duty
based on need it is submitted that the respective needs of the beneficiaries
under the will cannot be considered at the same level as that of the plaintiff.

128
After referring to the decision of Madam
Justice McLachlin, speaking for the court,
in
Tataryn v. Tataryn

(1994),
1994 CanLII 51 (SCC)
,
93 B.C.L.R. (2d) 145
at page 156
with regard to the moral duty owed,
counsel says:

Obviously this Court
must concern itself with the question as to whether there are circumstances
which negate the existence of such an obligation on the part of the testatrix
towards the Plaintiff, in reference to the reasons given by the testatrix, as
expressed in the will and as expressed as hearsay evidence through witnesses
called in the trial.

I agree, and it will be seen that in
my opinion the conduct of the plaintiff over the years clearly negated any
moral obligation to her on the part of Nettie.  In my opinion the surrounding
circumstances are capable of giving rise to no other reasonable conclusion.

129
In his written submission counsel again
deals with the reasons for disinheritance, the expressed reason in the will,
the plaintiff's influencing Peter Romaniuk to change his will in her favour,
the $40,000.00 loan and the estrangement from Nettie's grandchildren by the
plaintiff, and the validity and significance of the reasons.  I do not propose
to deal with these topics in detail again.  But I will make the following
observations at this time.  The expressed reason refers only to the plaintiff's
attempts to "deny" Nettie's inheritance following the death of Mr.
Romaniuk.  And while I am satisfied that I may consider other reasons, not
expressed in the will, I look upon the other reasons in this case simply as
other evidence of conduct on the part of the plaintiff, of the way in which she
treated Nettie over the years.  For example, I am satisfied that the plaintiff
and her husband probably sought a loan of $40,000.00 from Nettie and her
husband when the plaintiff and her husband decided to buy the ranch.  I am also
satisfied that the refusal was the cause of some bitterness, not on the part of
Nettie, but on the part of the plaintiff.

130
It is common ground that the plaintiff
preferred her father, and that he "went to the plaintiff" when he had
problems.  Nettie believed that the plaintiff was influential in Mr. Romaniuk
changing his will in her favour.  It is not known whether or not Mr. Romaniuk
acknowledged this to Nettie, or whether it was simply a matter of inference or
belief on her part.  Again, it is clear that at the material time Mr. Romaniuk
was not well.  And I do not place much weight on the assertion of influence by
the plaintiff on her father in his last year or so.

131
With regard to the estrangement from the
grandchildren, I am satisfied that it is more likely than not that the
grandchildren were influenced by the plaintiff to avoid Nettie.  The
alternative is that the grandchildren did this on their own, that is they chose
to side with their mother.  In any event I am satisfied that Nettie was not
allowed to go to Carol's wedding because the plaintiff would not permit her to
do so.  Again, this is simply evidence of the conduct of the plaintiff towards
Nettie over the years.

132
Finally counsel reiterated his earlier
argument that the plaintiff's conduct was not that of a daughter trying to take
her mother's inheritance, but one of a daughter trying to undo a wrong and to
vindicate her father's name.  The estrangement between the mother and daughter
says counsel was the result of the breakdown of her parents' marriage, and the
daughter's close relationship to the father, rather than the result of any
misconduct on the part of the plaintiff.  I do not agree.

133
Counsel finally deals with the issue of
need and the nature of Nettie's estate.  I have already stated my opinion that
the plaintiff is not in need in the circumstances of this case.  And as regards
Nettie's estate, it is made up mainly of the value in the family home which she
contributed to substantially, and probably more so than did Mr. Romaniuk.
Counsel also submits that the plaintiff should recover costs on Scale 3.  At
trial both counsel urged me to agree that the costs of all parties should come
out of the estate.  I do not agree that such is the case.  For, if that was the
practice it would encourage cases like the present one to be brought.  Costs
will be awarded to the party who succeeds, on Scale 3.

134
I turn now to the submissions of counsel
for the defendants.  The defence, says counsel, is as pleaded in paragraph 8 of
the defence, and which I have already reproduced in these reasons.  The
plaintiff's conduct has disentitled her to the benefit of an order under the
Act.  She sued Nettie to take away at least some of her inheritance, the
plaintiff and Nettie never reconciled after the lawsuit, and Nettie accurately
stated in her will why she disinherited the plaintiff.  Hence Nettie did not
misconstrue the rift between herself and her daughter.  The court must exercise
its discretion referred to in section 3 of the Act, and refuse to make an order
in favour of the plaintiff.  That section reads:

(3)The
court may attach the conditions to the order that it thinks fit, or may refuse
to make an order in favour of a person whose character or conduct, in the
court's opinion, disentitles him or her to the benefit of an order under this
Act.

135
Counsel continues, noting that following
Peter Romaniuk's death it quickly became apparent that the plaintiff was only
going to recover $4,000.00 in bonds.  Everything else had been transferred to
Nettie in the hospital.  It is true that the manner in which they were
transferred, i.e. with the nurse guiding Peter Romaniuk's hand, may not have
been "the way to do that", but once it had been done there was no
need for the plaintiff to do anything.  She did not even have to take out
probate.  Nettie was recovering everything, and according to the plaintiff that
was what she expected.

136
I will note here that I am alive to the
argument that the plaintiff was simply attempting to recover her own
inheritance from her father, as opposed to taking anything which rightfully
belonged to Nettie; and that accordingly Nettie's reason in her will was
neither rational nor valid.  It will be seen that I do not agree with such view
or interpretation of the plaintiff's conduct, or of Nettie's perception of it.
I am satisfied on the evidence, much of which I have reviewed, that Nettie's
view that the plaintiff was attempting to take her inheritance from her, even
before Mr. Romaniuk's death, and the subsequent trial, was clearly warranted.

137
Mrs. Ekdahl described the "family
feud", which occurred when Nettie discovered that Peter was going to
change or had changed his will in favour of the plaintiff.  Nettie was led to
believe that Peter subsequently made out a will in her favour.  In effect the
transfers executed at the hospital fulfilled Peter's promise and Nettie's
expectation.

138
The plaintiff testified that she wanted to
clear her father's name, but there was nothing to clear.  If she was referring
to the cheques being signed in dubious circumstances, no one else knew and no
one cared, except the plaintiff.  The fact is that the plaintiff took out
letters probate.  She then consulted counsel, and brought her action against
Nettie.  This was all calculated to get her father's estate and money into her
own hands.  She gave no thought to Nettie's needs of funds, a home, and a car.
Nettie had worked for many years, often when Mr. Romaniuk was not working, to
help produce and maintain those assets.  The fact that the plaintiff wanted the
money and estate for her own use is corroborated in a number of ways, including
her evidence at trial, the fact that she and her husband went to Nettie's home
and confronted her, and the very pleading in the action she brought.  She sued
Nettie for the money, a car, furniture, and tools.

139
The defendants do not rely on the fact
that the plaintiff and her husband sought a $40,000.00 loan from Nettie and her
husband.  They rely only on the positive acts taken by the plaintiff, mainly
suing Nettie for her father's estate.  Her evidence that she did not want the
money, car, and other assets, and that in effect, she had to sue Nettie, is
simply incomprehensible.

140
Counsel noted that following the trial the
parties went their separate ways, and there was very little contact, until
Nettie wrote to the plaintiff on July 11, 1989 apologizing, and seeking
permission to go to Carol's wedding.  She ended that letter with the words
"Kay if you want to write us.  We'd love to attend Carol and Mike's
wedding."  In this regard I am satisfied that it is more likely than not
that the plaintiff did not respond to the letter or the request.

141
Counsel also emphasized Mrs. Ekdahl's
evidence that Nettie was always wanting the plaintiff to respond to her overtures
to reconcile their differences.  He points out that she was rebuffed on at
least two occasions, when Carol was married, and later or before when another
grandchild was married, and Nettie stood outside during the reception or the
wedding.  The letter referred to also constituted an offer by Nettie to try and
reconcile.  The incident where Nettie met the plaintiff in a store, and the
plaintiff walked away refusing to talk to her, is another example of Nettie
trying unsuccessfully to reconcile with the plaintiff.  The same applies to the
incidents where the grandchildren did the same.

142
Any moral obligation on the part of Nettie
to make provision for the plaintiff in her will was drained or displaced.
Counsel relies both on
Bell
at page 42, and the decision of
Taggart, J.A., speaking for the majority of the Court of Appeal,
in
Price
v. Lypchuk
,
1987 CanLII 165 (BC CA)
,
[1987] 4 W.W.R. 128
, particularly at pages 137 and 138.

143
I turn briefly to counsel's written
submission.  While referring to the $40,000.00 loan, and to Nettie's conclusion
that the plaintiff and her first husband were plotting so as to transfer his
estate to the plaintiff, he reiterates that the plaintiff's action against
Nettie "with the objective of taking from her the small amount of Peter's
property received from him shortly before his death, totally justifies Nettie's
disinheritance of her daughter."  And he notes that the onus of proof is
on the plaintiff, to show that Nettie was incorrect in her assessment of the
facts.  Counsel again emphasizes that the plaintiff's explanation for suing her
mother is simply not acceptable, particularly in light of the fact that she had
consulted counsel, first to prove the will, and then to commence the action.
The pleadings, of course, speak for themselves.  He also notes that it is
patently obvious that the plaintiff's action against Nettie could not possibly
improve Peter Romaniuk's reputation or status in the eyes of others.  There is
only one obvious and real reason for the action, and that is that the plaintiff
wanted the money and property involved.

144
With regard to the question of
reconciliation counsel points out that the plaintiff admitted at trial that she
did not visit or even speak to Nettie for the 10 years preceding Nettie's
death.  The only grandchild that Nettie had social contact with was David, and
he eventually moved away.  An inference can be drawn that Nettie's two letters
were the only letters ever written between her and the plaintiff, and that
reconciliation never took place, as the conduct of the plaintiff alone
demonstrates.

145
Counsel also referred to Nettie's stay in
the hospital and the visits to her.  I do not find it necessary to consider
these matters.  They do not suggest reconciliation even at the hospital.
Finally, counsel submits that the plaintiff's claim be dismissed on the basis
that:

(a)The
Plaintiff has failed to prove that the testator was mistaken in her reasons for
disinheriting her daughter, or that the reason given was not adequate.

(b)Owing
to the Plaintiff's treatment of the testators she no longer owned (sic) the
Plaintiff the slightest part of a moral duty to support her adult child.

DISPOSITION

146
On December 8, 1991 Nettie Richardson died
at the age of 80 years.  She left her modest, hard earned estate to persons who
had loved and comforted her, and helped her one way or another.  They are a
sister, a nephew and a couple who were her neighbours.  None of them is a
person protected by the Act.  They are in law "strangers" to the
Act.  She did not leave anything to her relatives, who did not show it if they
loved her, and who in any event did not comfort and help her, but turned their
backs on her, her daughter the plaintiff and her grandchildren.  Her daughter
of course is the only person protected by the Act, and to whom it may be said
Nettie owed a duty.

147
The plaintiff seeks a discretionary order
pursuant to section 2(1) of the Act.  At the time of Nettie's death the
plaintiff was around 61 years of age.  She had not had anything to do with
Nettie for many years, and was in no way dependent upon her.  While she could
have used more money, like most persons, I find that she was not in need; and
note additionally that her own evidence suggested this to be the case.  This
leaves for consideration, in deciding the issue, the moral duty of Nettie to
the plaintiff, if any, Nettie's reasons for disinheriting the plaintiff,
particularly as to their accuracy, and, as well, the plaintiff's character or
conduct.

148
I have reviewed the evidence in some
detail.  There is no doubt that the plaintiff has been estranged from Nettie
for many years.  This probably began innocently enough in the earlier years
when, as she said, she loved both her parents, but favoured her father.  It
became more intense, if not irrevocable, when Nettie and her husband declined
to loan the $40,000.00 to the plaintiff and her husband, and even more so, at
the time that Mr. Romaniuk changed his will, and in which Nettie felt the
plaintiff was involved, and when the plaintiff sued Nettie to recover her
father's estate, as the plaintiff put it.  The unhappiness and hard feelings in
the main were on the part of the plaintiff, rather than Nettie, up to the time that
the plaintiff sued Nettie; because it is obvious that at the time of the will
changing incident Nettie understood that the matter had been resolved in her
favour.

149
After the lawsuit it appears that Nettie,
as well as the plaintiff, was not prepared to budge in the direction of a
reconciliation; although I have concluded on the evidence that it is more
likely than not that Nettie would have been prepared to reconcile with the
plaintiff in time, had any reasonable and sincere approach been made by the
plaintiff.  In any event, I am further satisfied that while the plaintiff
simply ignored and stayed away from Nettie for approximately nine years after
the trial, by the summer of 1989 Nettie was prepared to reconcile her differences
with the plaintiff.  She obviously loved her grandchildren and was simply dying
to go to Carol's wedding.  This is when she wrote what Mrs. Ekdahl described as
her "begging letter" dated July 11, 1989.  In her earlier 1987 letter
to the plaintiff she had suggested that it was time to bury the hatchet.  In
the July 11th letter she went farther.  She apologized to the plaintiff's
husband, expressed the hope that their relations had healed by then, and in
effect requested permission to go to Carol's wedding.  Her letter, which closed
with "Kay if you want to write us.  We would love to attend Carol and
Mike's wedding", is quite telling.  However, and contrary to the evidence
given and led on behalf of the plaintiff, I am satisfied that it is more likely
than not that the plaintiff never responded to the letter, and that it was made
clear to Nettie one way or another that she was not welcome at the wedding.  I
have concluded also that around this time, if not before, most of the
grandchildren had become estranged from Nettie, and that the plaintiff probably
had a hand in it.

150
On the evidence before me, and given the
history of the plaintiff's relationship with Nettie over the years, I do not
find it difficult to understand how Nettie could have concluded that the
plaintiff had a hand in the changing of her father's will, and in the
alienation of the grandchildren.  Further, and more importantly, in my opinion
the evidence is overwhelming that Nettie was warranted in her belief in her
reasons for disinheriting the plaintiff, that which is expressed in her will,
that the plaintiff attempted to deny her inheritance following the death of her
first husband, and the others which she related to the defendants, and were in
turn related by them to the court.  I will have more to say about this in a
moment.

151
I turn now to the law, and refer first to
the recent decision of the Court of Appeal
in
Bell v. Roy Estate
,

1993 CanLII 1262 (BC CA)
,
[1993] 4 W.W.R. 40
, wherein the judgment of the court was delivered by Mr.
Justice Goldie.  I look upon this case hopefully as some evidence of the Court
of Appeal moving back to a position where more emphasis or consideration is
given to why the testatrix (or testator) did what she did, and to what should
be her right or freedom to dispose of her property as she sees fit, absent
clear evidence of a violation of the Act on her part
viz
the unjustified
failure to "make adequate provision for the proper maintenance and support
of the testator's wife, husband or children" as the case may be, in her
will; and away from the much heavier emphasis which the courts have been
placing on the perceived views of the "reasonable testator", whose
every thought, often on matters which should be reflected in the legislation,
is a product of the judge rendering the decision.

152
In this regard the Court of Appeal said
per
curiam

in
Dennison v. Swain

(1965),
1965 CanLII 850 (BC CA)
,
54 W.W.R. 606
, at page
611
(I will leave out references to cases):

The learned judge ...
must have found that the testatrix had not acted in a judicious way to him and
was in manifest breach of her moral duty as a just parent.  Such a finding
could only be based on the conclusion that the testatrix had misjudged the
respondent and was wrong in making her provision for his proper maintenance by
way of an assured income from a fund for life rather than by way of a smaller
outright lump sum bequest.  With respect, I consider the learned judge erred in
principle in so concluding.
Although it is the duty of the court, as far as
possible, to place itself in all respects in the position of the testator for
the purpose of considering what ought to have been done by a just and wise
parent under the circumstances:
...
the greatest care should be taken to
appreciate the motives which swayed him in the disposition of his property or
the justification which might be apparent for his decisions
, and not merely
to make a new will for the testator.

(My emphasis)

153

In
Bell
Mr. Justice Goldie
states at page 47:

In the case at bar the
trial judge concluded that if the reasons the testatrix had in mind when she
disinherited her daughter were sustained those reasons were sufficient to
support the will.  He laid no particular stress on the size of the estate but
looked directly at the reasons Mrs. Roy did what she did and whether she was
warranted in her belief in those reasons for what she did.  There was evidence
which supported the finding she believed in the reasons stated.

I think he was right
both in this approach and in his finding that the burden then lay upon Mrs.
Bell to show that the reasons Mrs. Roy acted upon were false or unwarranted.
This places more emphasis on the intentions of the testatrix and less on those which
might be imputed to her by reference to the reasonable testator.  In my view
this is the correct conclusion to be drawn from the 1971 amendment to s. 2 of
the Act.

He then sets out the present
subsections (3) and (4) and continues:

Moreover, it is apparent
from subs. (4) that the weight to be given evidence of the testator's reasons
is affected by its accuracy and not by morally acceptable or unacceptable
content.  I do not say the legislature swept away any objectively determined
moral duty.  I do say, however, that the actual intentions of the testator are
to be given an effect which is largely denied by reliance upon the notionally
objective reasonable testator.

He then concludes:

... it follows the first
duty of a trial judge where no adequate provision has been made for a dependant
and need (as determined by the circumstances of the particular case) is not a
factor is to consider all the evidence of intention permitted under s. 2(3) of
the Act to determine whether the reasons so disclosed are rational and valid.
Where the answer to this inquiry supports the scheme of the will a court ought
to favour those intentions.

154
While the plaintiff is the only person
entitled to make a claim under section 2 of the Act, I decline to exercise my
discretion under section 2(1), to deprive Nettie of her freedom of testamentary
disposition, and to vary the terms of her will in favour of the plaintiff.
In
Price
v. Lypchuk
,
1987 CanLII 165 (BC CA)
,
[1987] 4 W.W.R. 128 (C.A.)
, Lambert, J.A., speaking for
himself and Taggart, J.A., said this, with regard to the moral duty owed by a
testator to those entitled to claim under the Act, at page 137:

But the moral duty imposed
by the Act does not require a testator who has been rejected by a member of his
family to ignore the rejection, nor does it require that all family members be
treated equally, even when all are in need and the estate is small.  If the
members of the family have, for their parts, treated the testator either more
considerably or less considerably, or if some of them are less well suited than
others for the "battle of life", or if the testator has made gifts to
family members during their lifetimes, then the moral duty of the testator may
be discharged or depleted.  The testator must be judicious; he need not be
impervious.

In the case at bar the plaintiff's
relationship with Nettie was somewhat acrimonious even before the first action
was brought.  And thereafter she simply had no relationship with Nettie, and
was not prepared to reconcile their differences even on Nettie's death bed,
unless it was on her terms.  It is my opinion therefore that their relationship
was effectively drained of any moral obligation on the part of Nettie long
before her death.  Alternatively, if my understanding of the discretion given
to the court under section 2(1) is incorrect, then I invoke the provisions of
section 3, and refuse to make an order in favour of the plaintiff on the
grounds that the plaintiff's conduct disentitles her to the benefit of an order
under the Act.

155
There is, of course, a second reason, an
even more important one, why in my opinion the plaintiff cannot succeed.  And that
is Nettie's reasons for disinheriting the plaintiff, and for making the
dispositions she in fact made to the legal strangers.  As I have already
indicated, there were a number of reasons, the main one being that which is
stated in her will and to which I have already referred in Nettie's words, i.e.
that the plaintiff had attempted to deny her inheritance following the death of
Mr. Romaniuk.  That reason alone is sufficient to dispose of this case.
However, the other reasons are also of some import and, although not necessary,
bolster it.

156
The onus is on the plaintiff to show that
the reasons acted upon by Nettie were "false or unwarranted."  The
plaintiff has not discharged this onus.  On the contrary, in my opinion the
evidence clearly showed that Nettie was warranted in her belief in the reasons
referred to, and that in the circumstances they were both rational and valid.
And it would be unjust for the court to override or interfere with Nettie's
distribution of her estate.

157
The action is dismissed, and with costs
for the reasons already given.
